group: Unit iv — Risk Assessment & Operational Safety
title: Hazard Identification & Operational Risk Assessment

questions.q: A hazard is best defined as:
options: An accident that has already happened
Anything with the potential to cause harm
questions.explain: Hazard = potential to harm. A moving train, 25 kV Overhead Equipment (OHE) and a crowded platform are all hazards.

questions.q: Risk is calculated as:
options: Likelihood of harm × Severity of harm
questions.explain: Risk answers two questions about a hazard: how likely is harm, and how bad would it be?

questions.q: Risk assessment is best described as:
options: A systematic process: identify hazards → who may be harmed and how → evaluate risk → decide controls → record → review
A form filled after an accident
questions.explain: Assessment happens before work, in this order, and ends with recording and review — not with a guess.

questions.q: Residual risk means:
options: A risk that cannot be identified
The risk remaining after controls are applied
questions.explain: Controls reduce risk; what remains is residual risk, and it must be As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP).

questions.q: As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) stands for:
questions.explain: As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP): keep reducing risk until further reduction would cost grossly more than the safety it buys.

questions.q: Which of these is an operational hazard in the book's list?
questions.explain: Operations looks for hazards in train movement, electricity, fire, crowd, falls, trespass and human factors.

questions.q: Which is a human-factor hazard?
questions.explain: Human factors — fatigue, distraction — are hazards just like electricity or weather.

questions.q: Hazard identification in operations uses which methods?
options: Inspections, job safety analysis, incident data, staff reporting and HAZID (Hazard Identification) / Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP) (Hazard and Operability Study) studies
questions.explain: Hazards are hunted actively: inspections, Job Safety Analysis (JSA), past incident data, staff reports and formal studies.

questions.q: HAZID (Hazard Identification) / Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP) (Hazard and Operability Study) studies are used especially when:
options: A new system is introduced or a change is made
questions.explain: New systems and changes get formal hazard studies because their hazards are not yet known from experience.

questions.q: Job Safety Analysis (JSA) examines:
options: A specific job, step by step, to find its hazards before work starts
questions.explain: Job Safety Analysis (JSA) breaks a job into steps and asks at each step: what can hurt here, and how do we control it?

questions.q: In a risk matrix, the two axes are:
options: Likelihood (rare to almost certain) and Severity (minor to catastrophic)
questions.explain: Every risk is placed on the matrix by how likely it is and how severe it would be.

questions.q: A risk rated High (red) in the matrix means:
options: It must be controlled before work proceeds
questions.explain: Red = control before work. The matrix is a decision tool, not a decoration.

questions.q: A Medium (amber) risk calls for:
questions.explain: Amber risks proceed only with controls in place and the risk watched.

questions.q: A Low (green) risk is managed by:
questions.explain: Green does not mean ignored — it means normal procedures are a sufficient control.

questions.q: Why must catastrophic severity never be ignored just because likelihood is low?
options: Because the matrix says so formally
Because if it happens, the consequences are unacceptable — low probability does not cancel catastrophic harm
questions.explain: A rare derailment or electrocution is still catastrophic. Severity keeps its vote in the assessment.

questions.q: A typical risk matrix is of what size?
options: 5 × 5 — five likelihood levels by five severity levels
questions.explain: The book teaches the typical 5×5 matrix behind the low/medium/high/extreme bands.

questions.q: In the book's banding, a High risk requires:
options: Stopping — a senior decision before proceeding
questions.explain: High = stop and escalate; the decision to proceed sits at senior level with proper controls.

questions.q: An Extreme/Intolerable risk means:
options: Work must not proceed at all
questions.explain: Intolerable is the red line: no controls discussion — the work simply does not start.

questions.q: The correct order of the risk-assessment process is:
options: Identify hazards → decide who may be harmed and how → evaluate the risk → decide controls → record → review
Decide controls → identify hazards → record → evaluate → review
questions.explain: Assessment flows from finding hazards to controlling them, then writing it down and reviewing it.

questions.q: When must a risk assessment be reviewed?
options: Never — once done it is final
When conditions change, after incidents, and as part of the regular review cycle
questions.explain: A stale assessment describes a railway that no longer exists; change and incidents trigger review.

questions.q: Staff reporting contributes to hazard identification because:
options: Front-line staff see hazards in daily work that inspections may miss
questions.explain: The person doing the job daily is a hazard sensor — reporting channels turn their observations into controls.

questions.q: Incident data helps risk assessment by showing:
options: Which hazards have already caused harm or near-misses, and how often
questions.explain: Past incidents and near-misses are evidence of likelihood — the matrix is fed by real data.

questions.q: Scenario: A wet, slippery platform in the rainy season. The hazard and risk are:
options: Hazard: wet surface; risk: likelihood of falls × severity of injuries to passengers
questions.explain: Separate the two words: the wet platform is the hazard; the chance and consequence of a fall is the risk.

questions.q: Extreme weather appears in hazard identification as:
options: An operational hazard affecting safe working
questions.explain: Extreme weather can create hazards across the railway — it belongs in the hazard list.

questions.q: Objects on the track and trespassers are examples of:
questions.explain: Anything that can cause harm — a trespasser, a fallen object — is identified and assessed as a hazard.

questions.q: Interface failures are listed as hazards because:
options: Where systems meet (train–platform, Operations Control Centre (OCC)–field), failures can create harm
Interfaces are not part of operations
questions.explain: Hazards hide at interfaces: Platform Screen Door (PSD)–train, Operations Control Centre (OCC)–station, power–train. Assessment must look there specifically.

questions.q: What does 'who may be harmed and how' add to hazard identification?
options: It turns a general hazard into specific risks for specific people
questions.explain: A live wire is a hazard; 'track staff may touch it during maintenance' is the risk picture that drives controls.

questions.q: As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) requires risk to be reduced until:
options: Further reduction would cost grossly more than the safety gained
questions.explain: As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) is a balance with a thumb on the safety side: stop reducing only when the cost is grossly disproportionate.

questions.q: Scenario: A hazard is very unlikely but would kill many people if it occurred. Correct treatment:
options: Mention it in a footnote only
Assess and control it seriously — catastrophic severity is never dismissed for low likelihood
Wait for it to happen once
questions.explain: Likelihood is only half the product. Catastrophic × rare still demands real controls.

questions.q: Recording the risk assessment matters because:
options: It makes the decisions traceable and reviewable, and shows controls were decided before work
It is needed only for audits
questions.explain: If it is not recorded, it cannot be reviewed, checked or learned from.

questions.q: Which is the best source for spotting a hazard in an existing operation?
options: A combination of inspections, incident/near-miss data and staff reporting
questions.explain: No single method sees everything — inspections, data and front-line reports together give the full picture.

questions.q: A hazard is different from a risk because:
options: A hazard is the potential to cause harm; risk is the likelihood and severity of that harm occurring
A hazard is always an accident
questions.explain: Exam favourite: hazard = potential; risk = likelihood × severity of that potential becoming real.

questions.q: Fire and smoke in a station are treated in hazard identification as:
options: Hazards whose risk is assessed for passengers and staff
questions.explain: Fire/smoke can kill quickly in enclosed stations — it is a core operational hazard.

questions.q: Crowd crush on a platform is:
options: A hazard arising from crowd density at the platform
questions.explain: Crowd crush is listed among operational hazards — density itself can injure and kill.

questions.q: Before introducing a changed working method, the correct safety step is:
options: Assess the risks of the change (e.g., Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP)-style review/Job Safety Analysis (JSA)) before it goes live
No assessment is needed for small changes
questions.explain: Change creates new hazards; assessment precedes introduction, not the first accident after it.

questions.q: The output of a risk assessment should directly decide:
options: What controls are needed for the work to proceed safely
questions.explain: Assessment is not academic — its output is the control set for the job.

questions.q: Scenario: Likelihood 'rare', severity 'catastrophic', no controls yet. The matrix position demands:
options: Serious controls and senior attention before the activity proceeds
A note in the log book only
questions.explain: Catastrophic severity pulls the risk up the matrix even at low likelihood — control it before proceeding.

questions.q: Why does the assessment ask for severity 'of harm', not 'of damage cost'?
options: Because the matrix measures harm to people first, not money
questions.explain: Severity is about injury and death first — that is why punctuality and cost never outrank it.

questions.q: A risk that remains after all planned controls is the:
options: Residual risk, which must be As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) and accepted knowingly
questions.explain: You work with residual risk every day — the duty is to make it As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) and know what remains.

questions.q: In operational risk assessment, which pairing of step and tool is correct?
options: Hazard identification — the matrix; Risk evaluation — Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
Hazard identification — inspections and HAZID; Risk evaluation — the likelihood × severity matrix
questions.explain: First find and list the hazards, then score each one on the matrix to decide controls.

questions.q: A hazard log (hazard register) is maintained throughout the life of a railway system in order to:
options: Record every identified hazard with its assessed risk, the controls applied and its current status, so no known hazard is ever lost track of
questions.explain: Hazards are identified over years by many different people. The hazard log is the system's memory: each hazard, its risk, its controls and whether it is closed or still open — reviewed whenever anything changes.

questions.q: A Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP) examines a system mainly by:
options: Watching it run for one day
Applying guide words such as 'No', 'More', 'Less' and 'Reverse' to each part of the design to systematically find deviations from the intended operation
questions.explain: Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP) is structured imagination: for each element, the team asks what happens if there is NO flow, MORE pressure, LESS speed, REVERSE movement — and whether the result can cause harm. It finds hazards before the system is ever built or changed.

questions.q: A Job Safety Analysis (JSA) is done by:
options: Reading the accident reports of other railways
Breaking a specific job into its steps and identifying the hazards and precautions at each step before the job is done
questions.explain: Job Safety Analysis (JSA) looks at one real job — say, cleaning a Platform Screen Door (PSD) track-side sensor — step by step: where can a hand slip, what is live, what can move? Each step gets its precaution before work starts, not after an injury.

questions.q: In a bow-tie diagram of a hazard, the 'top event' sits in the centre with:
options: Threats and preventive barriers on the left, and consequences with recovery barriers on the right
questions.explain: The bow-tie shows the whole story of one hazard: what can cause the loss-of-control event, what stops it happening, and if it happens anyway, what limits the damage. Weak or missing barriers are visible at a glance.

questions.q: In risk tolerability terms, a risk assessed as 'intolerable' must be:
options: Accepted if the service is important
Reduced regardless of cost, or the activity must not be carried out — it cannot be justified by benefits
questions.explain: Above the intolerable line there is no bargaining: the risk comes down or the activity stops. Only below that line does As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) begin, where further reduction is balanced against grossly disproportionate cost.
